prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: B005 is the one candidate that nearly the whole committee ranks near the top (seven of eight in the top three), and I think that reflects substance and not just overlap in taste. The idea can be explained with one picture: choose the wavelength of the trapping light so that it shifts both clock levels equally, and thousands of atoms can be held in a lattice without Doppler or recoil shifts. The payoff is a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, which lets us see gravitational redshift across a millimetre and tighten limits on varying constants and on some dark-matter couplings. As a theorist I note that the magic wavelengths and the blackbody-radiation shift are a case where atomic many-body calculations and measurement meet at a precision few other fields reach. The work has been reproduced and surpassed in many laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and others), and clock comparisons between institutes are routine, so the result does not rest on one measurement. Katori's proposal and first strontium clock, together with Ye's push to record accuracy and Fermi-degenerate many-body clocks, give a clean two-name attribution that all eight colleagues proposed independently.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty. The 2005 prize recognised the frequency comb and the 2012 prize recognised the control of single trapped ions, so a sceptic can call the lattice clock an excellent refinement of already honoured measurement science, and part of its significance is still prospective until the SI second is redefined. There is also a legitimate worry about credit: Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and Derevianko, among others, made essential contributions that two names cannot capture. If the committee wants a clearly new discovery about nature instead of a measurement advance, B015 or B014 would answer that better.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B005 first but raises the scope question: should the prize be tied to the clock invention or to the broader frequency-comb and precision-metrology lineage already recognised in 2005?
responses.response: I would keep the citation tied narrowly to the lattice clock. The comb is the ruler that reads out the optical oscillations. The magic-wavelength lattice is what removes the motional and light shifts and so gives the clock its stability. That is a distinct idea, and the citation I propose reflects it. I share your concern about the priority chronology, but I would treat it as a drafting matter for the citation and not as a reason to broaden the prize.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Car-Parrinello B043 first, arguing it is original and enormously influential, and that the open question is whether a computational method counts as a physical discovery of the kind Nobel physics usually requires.
responses.response: I respect the impact, and as a theorist who builds calculations I do not look down on computation. My reservation is the one you raise yourself. Car and Parrinello gave us a tool, and the 1998 chemistry prize for density functional theory already covers much of its foundation. The lattice clock is also an invention, but it opens a measurement regime and delivers physical results such as redshift tests and constraints on constants. B043 had a single first-place vote and no other support, so I would put it behind B005 and would want a stronger argument for why it is a physics discovery before treating it as a competitor.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics B051 first because it is a decisive instrumentation advance that changed what can be seen, and she also flags that her own field affinity may bias her weighting.
responses.response: I agree about the importance. Seeing individual atoms routinely is a great achievement, and I accept that instrument building is part of the Nobel tradition. But B051 reached only one first-place vote and no other member ranked it, so the committee has little independent view of it, and I cannot judge the credit among Rose, Haider, Urban and the scanning-microscope corrector groups. I would also ask whether it reveals something new about nature or improves our ability to look. B005 is an instrument too, but it also enables new tests of physics, and it has a much wider base of support.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube B035 first as detector development leading to discovery, with a real new observational window, while noting the attribution problem inside a large collaboration.
responses.response: I find the science of B035 compelling, since a new window onto the sky is exactly the kind of discovery I value, and I defer to you and Danielsson on astroparticle physics. My caution is attribution and maturity. Source identifications such as TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 rest on moderate statistical significance, and a three-name prize for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND as precursors, will always be contestable. I am not saying it should not win, only that B005 is cleaner on both counts today. Do you think the diffuse flux alone is enough to carry a citation?

responses.point: Mehlig ranks KPZ B016 first as a minimal model defining a universality class, linking growth, random matrices and integrable probability, with clean experimental checks in liquid-crystal convection.
responses.response: The elegance is real and I like the connection to Tracy-Widom statistics. My concern is the credit: Parisi is already recognised and not credited, and the exact solutions you cite came from a wide group (Johansson, Sasamoto, Spohn, Amir, Corwin, Quastel). Only one member ranked it, and it lies outside my field, so I cannot judge it as I can an atomic-physics candidate. I would want to understand whether Kardar and Zhang alone are the right pair before treating it as a serious competitor.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues weigh the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as making the lattice clock incremental, and how much the pending SI second redefinition should matter for timing.
Whether two names fully capture credit for the lattice clock given Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and Derevianko.

Whether a second, distinct achievement, for example B015 (cold-atom quantum simulation) or B014 (moire quantum matter), should share the prize, and within B015 whether Zoller, Esslinger or Greiner should take the third seat.
I have not independently verified the priority chronology or the latest accuracy figures and am working from recollection.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored papers with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and I know Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato through storage-ring and precision-atomic work. None of this involves Katori, Ye, or the other shortlisted candidates, so no specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B005, although my closeness to the atomic-physics community around B015 may be worth noting.
